solicitude.e: From Middle English solicitude, from Old French sollicitude, from Latin sollicitūdō (“anxiety”), from sollicitus, solicitus (“anxious, solicitous”). See solicitous.
solicitude.x: For there to be genuine community among any sizable group of people, solicitude must be a routine feature of daily intercourse.

solidarity.e: By surface analysis, from English solidary + -ity, or from French solidarité (“solidarity”), from solidaire (“characterized by solidarity”), from Latin solidum (“whole…
solidarity.x: A long time union member himself, Phil showed solidarity with the picketing grocery store workers by shopping at a competing, unionized store.

solidify.e: From French solidifier. By surface analysis, solid + -ify.
solidify.x: Emerging from Kennaway Tunnel, the train sweeps to the right, affording views of the recent work to solidify the railway here.

soliloquy.e: 1595–1605; From Late Latin sōliloquium in the title of St. Augustine's Soliloquiorum libri duo ("Two Books of Soliloquies"), from sōlus (“only, sole”) + loquor (“to…
soliloquy.x: At the end of the second act the main villain gave a soliloquy detailing his plans to attack the protagonist.

solitary.e: From Middle English solitarie, borrowed from Latin sōlitārius. Doublet of solitaire.

solitude.e: From Middle English solitude, from Old French solitude, from Latin sōlitūdō. By surface analysis, sole + -itude.
solitude.x: Cranks like Rousseau made solitude glamorous, but sensible people agreed that it was really terrible.

solstice.x: The point at which the sun is nearest to the south pole we call the winter solstice, and the opposite point, the summer solstice.

soluble.e: From Middle English soluble, from Old French soluble, from Late Latin solūbilis, from Latin solvere (“to loosen”) + -bilis. Piecewise doublet of solvable.
soluble.x: That mystery should be easily soluble.

solvable.e: From solve + -able. Piecewise doublet of soluble. More information The mathematical senses derive from Galois theory: Galois discovered that one could determine whether a…
solvable.x: Questions of this Nature may be easily solvable in the simple Cases.

solvent.e: From French solvent, from Latin solventem, accusative singular of solvens, present participle of solvō. By surface analysis, solv(e) + -ent.
solvent.x: It explains. And explanation is the true solvent of mystery.

sombre.e: Borrowed from French sombre (“dark”), from Old French sombre, from a verb *sombrer or Latin sub- + umbra. Compare Spanish sombra (“shade; dark part of a picture; ghost”).
sombre.x: The dinner was silent and sombre; happily it was also short.

sombrero.e: Borrowed from Spanish sombrero (“hat”), from sombra (“shadow, shade”) + -ero, literally, "shade-maker". The drink was named after the hat.

somersault.e: From French sombresault (now obsolete, compare French sursaut, soubresaut), from Old Occitan sobresalt, from sobre- (“over, above”) + salt (“jump”), from Latin suprā…

somnambulism.e: From French somnambulisme, from New Latin somnambulus, from Latin somnus (“sleep”) + ambulō (“to walk”), + -ism.

somnambulist.e: Borrowed from French somnambuliste, from Medieval Latin somnambulus (“sleepwalker”). By surface analysis, somn- + -ambulist.

sonar.x: They were able to detect the sunken wreck using sonar.

sonata.e: From Italian sonata, from the feminine past participle of sonare (modern suonare), from Latin sonāre (“to make sound”). Doublet of sounded.

songbook.e: From Middle English song boke, from Old English sangbōc (“a music book; songbook”), equivalent to song + book.

songster.e: From Middle English songster, sangester, sangstere, from Old English sangestre (“a female singer; songstress”), equivalent to song + -ster.
songster.x: A member of a Salvation Army family, she had been a songster accompanying the band around the streets of Chelmsford where she lived with her parents.

songstress.e: From songster + -ess. Compare West Frisian sjongeres (“songstress”), Dutch zangeres (“songstress”).
songstress.x: The songstress paused, and was answered by one or two deep and hollow groans, that seemed to proceed from the very agony of the mortal strife.

songwriter.x: We are now collaborating with a famous songwriter.

sonnet.e: Borrowed from Middle French sonnet, from Italian sonetto, from Old Occitan sonet (“a song”), diminutive of son (“song, sound”), from Latin sonus (“sound”).

sonorous.e: Borrowed from Latin sonōrus, from sonor (“sound”), early 17th century.
sonorous.x: The highlight of the hike was the sonorous cave, which produced a ringing echo from the hiker’s shouts.

soothsayer.e: From Middle English sothsaier, zothziggere, by surface analysis, sooth (“truth”) + sayer.

sooty.e: From Middle English sooty, soty, equivalent to soot + -y. Probably influenced by similar Middle English suti (“dirty, filthy”), derived from the same root as Old English…
sooty.x: The grisly legions that troop under the sooty flag of Acheron.

sophisticated.e: First English usage circa 1601. From Medieval Latin sophisticatus.

soprano.e: Borrowed from Italian soprano, from Vulgar Latin *superānus, adjective from preposition Latin super (“above”).
soprano.x: I was only once faced with the task of auditioning a nimiety of sopranos.

sorbet.x: After dinner we had an orange sorbet that was very refreshing.

sorcerer.e: From Middle English sorcerere, from stem sorcer- (as in sorceresse and sorcery) + -ere, from Old French sorcer, sorcier, from Early Medieval Latin sortiārius, derived…
sorcerer.x: Pope Joan, who once occupied the throne of the Vatican, was reputed to be the blackest sorcerer of them all.

sorceress.e: From Middle English sorceresse, from Anglo-Norman sorceresse.
sorceress.x: Perch: In the head of this fish there are small stones that sorceresses used in concocting love-philtres.

sorcery.e: From Middle English sorcery, borrowed from Middle French sorcerie, ultimately derived from Latin sors (“fate”), from Proto-Indo-European *ser- (“to bind”).
sorcery.x: The tale is full of magic and sorcery.

sordid.x: The politician was involved in a sordid money laundering scheme.

sorghum.e: From New Latin genus name Sorghum, from Italian sorgo, from Vulgar Latin *syricum (“Syrian”), from Sȳricus.

sorority.e: PIE word *swésōr From Renaissance Latin sorōritās, from Latin soror (“sister”), from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.
sorority.x: Every day is a party at this sorority!

sorrel.e: From Middle English sorel, from Old French sorel, surele (“sorrel”), from Old French sur (“sour”), of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sūraz (“sour”).

sorrowful.e: From Middle English sorweful, from Old English sorhful, sorgful (“full of care; anxious; sorrowful”), from Proto-Germanic *surgafullaz (“full of care.

sortie.e: PIE word *upó The noun is borrowed from French sortie (“act of exiting; exit, way out.
sortie.x: They are vastly outnumbered: Russia is believed to fly some 200 sorties per day while Ukraine flies five to 10.

soulless.e: From Middle English soulelez; equivalent to soul + -less. Compare Old English sāwollēas; the Middle English word likely is a re-formation.
soulless.x: “Done?” he said, with a soulless sneer in the word.

soulmate.e: From soul + mate. First attested as soul-mate in an 1822 letter by Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Not in common usage before the 1980s.
soulmate.x: Finding your wonderful soulmate is very similar to the process of sowing a seed and nurturing it into a beautiful blossoming plant.

soundless.x: The whole building, with its dark windows and soundless avenues, had an air strikingly forlorn and solitary.

soundproof.x: The contestant was placed in a soundproof booth so he could not receive help from the audience.

sourdough.e: From Middle English sour dogh, equivalent to sour + dough. Compare Saterland Frisian Suurdee (“sourdough”), Dutch zuurdeeg (“sourdough”), Low German Suurdeeg…

sourness.e: From Middle English sowrenesse, sournesse, from Old English sūrnes (“sourness”), equivalent to sour + -ness.
sourness.x: Mrs. Ferrars was a little, thin woman, upright, even to formality, in her figure, and serious, even to sourness, in her aspect.

southeast.e: From Middle English southest, from Old English sūþēast, equivalent to south + east.

southeastern.e: From Middle English *southesterne, from Old English sūþēasterne, equivalent to south + eastern.
southeastern.x: The southeastern part of the country is the most affluent.

southernmost.x: South Africa is the southernmost country in Africa.

southwest.e: From Middle English southwest, southewest, from Old English sūþwest and sūþanwestan, equivalent to south + west.

southwestern.e: From Middle English southwesterne, from Old English sūþwesterne, equivalent to south + western.
southwestern.x: Locals think southwestern sunsets are the most beautiful.

souvenir.e: Unadapted borrowing from French souvenir (literally “memory”). Compare memento.

sovereign.e: From Middle English sovereyn, from Old French soverain (whence also modern French souverain), from Vulgar Latin *superānus (compare Italian sovrano, Spanish soberano)…

sovereignty.e: PIE word *upér From Late Middle English sovereynte, souvereynte [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman sovereyneté, soverentee, and Old French soveraineté, souveraineté…

sovkhoz.e: From Russian совхо́з (sovxóz), abbreviation of сове́тское хозя́йство (sovétskoje xozjájstvo, “soviet farm”).

sower.e: From Middle English sowere, from Old English sāwere; equivalent to sow + -er.

spaceship.e: space + ship * (programming operator): From its resemblance to the shape of a flying saucer.
spaceship.x: The spaceships look like a row of threshers harvesting a field of wheat; the thickness in the direction of motion is only about 10 cells.

spacetime.e: From space + time, as a calque of German Raumzeit, introduced in this sense by Hermann Minkowski. First appears in print c. 1893 in the Philosophical Review.
spacetime.x: An event is a point in spacetime, specified by the coordinates x, y, z, and t.

spacious.e: From Middle English spacious, from Old French spacios, from Latin spatiōsus. By surface analysis, space + -ious.
spacious.x: The apartment has a spacious bedroom.

spade.e: From Middle English spade, from Old English spada, spade, spadu (“spade”), from Proto-Germanic *spadô. Doublet of spatha, spathe, and épée.
spade.x: I've got only one spade in my hand.

spaghetti.x: Her mother was cooking spaghetti for dinner.

spangle.e: The noun is derived from Middle English spangel (“small piece of ornamental metal, spangle.
spangle.x: Spangle butterfly (Papilio protenor) photographed in Tokyo, Japan.

spank.e: Uncertain. Possibly imitative, or perhaps a special use of Etymology 2 (below) in the sense of a horse stamping its foot against the ground.
spank.x: The ship was really spanking along.

spanner.x: Pass me that spanner, Jake; there's just one more bolt to screw in.

spark.e: Probably Scandinavian, akin to Old Norse sparkr (“sprightly”).
spark.x: When the latter disk showed some sparks, Moman contacted MGM's Jim Vienneau, who picked up the waxing for national release.

sparkle.e: From Middle English sparkel, sparkle, sparcle, equivalent to spark + -le (diminutive suffix). In some modern uses deverbal from etymology 2 below.
sparkle.x: The shock was sufficiently strong to strike out some sparkles of his fiery temper.

sparkler.x: And yet a married woman, possessing your attractions, shuts her eyes (and sparklers too), and goes and runs her delicate-formed head against a wall.

sparrow.x: Man progresses generally, not both legs at once like a sparrow, but by putting one leg forward first, and then the other.

spasm.e: From Middle English spasme, from Old French spasme, from Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm, convulsion”), from σπάω (spáō, “to draw out, pull…
spasm.x: Jessica went into spasms after eating a peanut.

spate.e: The noun is derived from Middle English spate, spait (“a flood”), influenced by Scots spate (“torrent of water, flood; heavy downpour of rain.
spate.x: Doun comes a jaw o' droukin' rain / Upon their honours— / God sends a spate outower the plain, / Or mebbe thun'ers.

spatter.e: Probably from Middle Low German or Dutch spatten (“to spout, burst”) + -er (frequentative suffix). Related to spit (“saliva”).
spatter.x: When my wet chihuahua shook himself, I was spattered with smelly water.

spatula.e: Borrowed from Latin spatula (“a flat piece”), the diminutive form of spatha (“broad or flat tool”), from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē, “a broad wood or metal blade”).
spatula.x: The croupier delicately faced her other two cards with the tip of his spatula. A four! She had lost!

spawn.e: From Middle English spawne, from the verb (see above).
spawn.x: This dreadful idea is the spawn of a large business conglomerate.

spearhead.e: From Middle English spere-hed; equivalent to spear + head.

spearmint.e: From spear (“sprout of a plant, spire”) + mint, so named due to its spiry blooms.

specialist.e: Borrowed from French spécialiste, equivalent to special + -ist.

specialization.x: A triangle is a specialization of a polygon to one with exactly three sides.

specialize.x: These cells specialized for propagation, however they may originate, are accordingly distinguished by a special name, that of Spores of Sporules.

specially.e: From Middle English specialli, specially, equivalent to special + -ly.
specially.x: We had this cake made specially for your birthday.

specialty.e: From Middle English specialte, Old French specialte, especialte, from Latin specialitas.
specialty.x: They cook well overall, but their true specialty is pasta.

specification.e: From Middle French specification, from Medieval Latin specificationem (accusative of specificatio).
specification.x: The contractor followed the architect’s specifications.

specificity.e: From specific + -ity, perhaps modelled after French spécificité. First attested in 1829.

specify.e: From Middle English specifien, from Old French specifier, especefier, or directly from Medieval Latin specificō, from specificus (“specific”).

specimen.e: From Latin specimen (“mark, sign, example”), from speciō (“observe, watch”).
specimen.x: "You're a nice specimen for a clergyman," he said at length, "with your preachin" an" your psalm-singin', an" your Sunday coat on."

specious.e: From Middle English speciose, specious, from Anglo-Norman specious, Middle French specieux, and their etymon Latin speciōsus (“good-looking”).
specious.x: This idea that we must see through what we have started is specious, however good it may sound.

speck.e: From Middle English spekke, from Old English specca (“small spot, stain”), from the same ultimate source as Proto-Germanic *sprakô (“spark”).

speckled.x: The bird's eggs were speckled as camouflage.

spectacle.e: From Middle English spectacle, from Middle French spectacle, from Latin spectāculum (“a show, spectacle”), from spectō (“to see, behold”), frequentative of speciō (“to…
spectacle.x: The horse race was a thrilling spectacle.

spectacles.x: He needed to get new spectacles because his original ones had broken.

spectator.e: Borrowed from Latin spectātor, from frequentative verb spectō (“watch”), from speciō (“look at”). Equivalent to spectate + -or. Doublet of speculator.
spectator.x: The cheering spectators watched the fireworks.

specter.e: From Middle French spectre, from Latin spectrum (“appearance, apparition”). Doublet of spectrum.
specter.x: A specter haunted the cemetery at the old Vasquez manor.

spectrum.x: Current 3G technologies can send roughly 1 bit of data - a one or a zero - per second over each 1 Hz of spectrum that the operator owns.

speculate.e: Borrowed from Latin speculātus, perfect active participle of speculor (“to watch, observe, examine, spy”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from specula (“a watchtower”)…
speculate.x: We can speculate that in many instances the sharks are not feeding on their victims, but only in a few cases can we guess what they are doing.

speculation.e: From Middle English speculacioun, speculation, from Old French speculation (compare French spéculation), from Late Latin speculātiō, speculātiōnem, from Latin speculor.
speculation.x: Thenceforth to speculations high or deep I turned my thoughts.

speculative.e: Inherited from Middle English speculatyf, borrowed from Old French speculatif or directly from Late Latin speculativus, from Latin speculor.
speculative.x: Like The Handmaid's Tale, Oryx and Crake is a speculative fiction, not a science fiction proper.

speculator.e: From Latin speculātor (“spy, explorer, investigator”), from speculor (“to watch, to observe”) + -tor (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from specula (“watchtower”), from…

speechless.e: From Middle English specheles, from Old English sprǣċlēas (“speechless; without the power of speak”), from Proto-Germanic *sprēkalausaz, equivalent to speech + -less.
speechless.x: When he walked into his surprise birthday party, he was completely speechless.

speedometer.e: From speed + -o- + -meter; by surface analysis, speed + -ometer.

spellbound.x: The story left the children spellbound.

spelling.x: For the practical use of spelling comes in writing.

spelt.e: From Middle English spelt, from Old English spelt (“spelt, corn”), from Old Saxon spelta (“spelt”); or from Late Latin spelta (“spelt”), from Frankish *spelta (“spelt”).

spendthrift.e: From spend + thrift (“(archaic) savings; profits; wealth”).

sperm.e: From Middle English sperme, from Latin sperma, from Ancient Greek σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, semen”). Compare also Old French esperme, sparme.
sperm.x: Out of two hundred million sperm, one penetrates the egg.

spermaceti.e: From Latin sperma (“sperm”) + Latin cētī (“of the whale”, genitive of cētus).

sphere.x: Of celestial bodies, first the sun, / A mighty sphere, he framed.

spherical.e: English spheric [from Latin sphaericus, from Ancient Greek σφαιρικός (sphairikós)] + -al.
spherical.x: Knaves, thieves, and treachers by spherical predominance.

sphinx.e: From Sphinx, from Middle English Spynx, from Latin Sphinx, from Ancient Greek Σφίγξ (Sphínx), perhaps either from σφίγγω (sphíngō, “to squeeze, to strangle”) (whence also…

spiced.x: Fred preferred spiced rum to plain.

spicy.x: This curry is too spicy for me. I can't eat it.

spiderweb.e: From Middle English spiþere webb, equivalent to spider + web.

spill.x: I spilled some sticky juice on the kitchen floor.

spinach.e: From Middle English spinach, from Anglo-Norman spinache, from Old French espinoche, from Old Occitan espinarc, from Arabic إِسْفَانَاخ (ʔisfānāḵ), from Classical Persian…
spinach.x: Another option is to wash spinach and other leafy greens thoroughly in running water before eating them.

spinal.e: Borrowed from Late Latin spīnālis (“of or belonging to the spine”), from spīna (“a prickle, spine”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). By surface analysis, spine + -al.

spindle.e: From Middle English spyndel, spindle, spyndylle, from Old English spindle, spindel, alteration of earlier spinel, spinil, spinl (“spindle”), from Proto-West Germanic…
spindle.x: Anna Pavlovna’s soirée was now in full swing. On all sides the spindles were humming away non-stop.

spine.e: From late Middle English spyne, from Old French espine (French épine) or its source, Latin spīna (“a thorn; a prickle, spine; the backbone”). Doublet of spina.
spine.x: The male, as Dr. Gunther informs me, has a cluster of stiff, straight spines, like those of a comb, on the sides of the tail.

spiral.e: From Middle French spirale, from Medieval Latin spiralis, from Latin spīra, from Ancient Greek σπεῖρα (speîra, “wreath, coil, twist”).
spiral.x: My beloved friends and family who sustained and grounded me as I fell into the rabbit hole of this project or down the spiral of new parenthood.

spire.e: From Middle English spire, spyre, spier, spir, from Old English spīr, from Proto-Germanic *spīrō, *spīrǭ (“peak; point; tip; stalk”).
spire.x: Clara had pulled a button from a hollyhock spire, and was breaking it to get the seeds.

spiritualism.x: What is called spiritualism should, I think, be called a mental species of materialism.

spirituality.x: If this light be not spiritual, yet it approacheth nearest unto spirituality.

spite.e: From Middle English spit, a shortening of despit (whence despite), from Old French despit, from Latin dēspectum (“looking down on”), from Latin dēspiciō (“to look down…
spite.x: He was so filled with spite for his ex-wife, his brother was afraid of what he might do.

spiteful.e: From Middle English spytefulle. By surface analysis, spite + -ful.

spittle.e: Alteration of dialectal spattle (by association with spit (noun)), from Old English spātl, which is related to spǣtan (whence spit (verb)).
spittle.x: "Who are you?!" he blurted into the woman's palm, and she shook it off in obvious disgust, wiping spittle onto his D-class uniform.

spleen.e: From Middle English splene, splen, from Anglo-Norman espleen and Old French esplein, esplen, from Latin splēn (“milt”), from Ancient Greek σπλήν (splḗn, “the spleen”).

splendor.e: From Anglo-Norman splendur, splendour, or directly from its source Latin splendor, from the verb splendeō (“to shine”).
splendor.x: The splendor of the Queen's coronation was without comparison.

splice.e: Circa 1525, borrowed from Middle Dutch splissen (Modern Dutch splitsen).
splice.x: If the ball hits the splice, it is likely to dolly up for an easy catch.

splinter.e: From Middle English splenter, splinter, from Middle Dutch splinter, equivalent to splint + -er.

spoiled.x: The child was spoiled by constant gifts.

spoiler.x: The optimism at the opening of the talks could not be dampened even by a few spoilers.

spoilsport.e: From the verbal expression spoil sport (“ruin the amusement”).
spoilsport.x: I know I am a sad spoilsport, but it would make me wretched.

spoilt.x: The food went spoilt in the heat and had to be thrown away.

spokesperson.e: From spoke (“past participle of speak”) + -s- + person.

sponge.e: From Middle English sponge, from Old English spunge, taken from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá), from σπόγγος (spóngos).

sponsor.e: Learned borrowing from Latin spōnsor (“a surety", in Late Latin "a sponsor in baptism”).
sponsor.x: He was my sponsor when I applied to join the club.

sponsorship.x: I find that for me, my sponsorship of a child via a charitable NGO provides a sense of great satisfaction.

spontaneity.e: From Latin spontaneus (“voluntary”). By surface analysis, spont(aneous) + -aneity. Compare French spontanéité.
spontaneity.x: In any case, they are not very big on spontaneity. They sit on him for a few minutes before they decide what to do next.

spontaneous.x: He made a spontaneous offer of help.

spontaneously.x: The idea that the body could spontaneously ignite was promoted by the 19th-century temperance movement.

spook.e: Borrowed from Dutch spook (“ghost”), from Middle Dutch spooc (“spook, ghost”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *spōk.
spook.x: The building was haunted by a couple of spooks.

spool.e: From Middle English spole (possibly via Old Northern French spole, espole), from Middle Dutch spoele, from Old Dutch *spōla, *spuola, from Proto-Germanic *spōlǭ…
spool.x: If you need to reload film, the cassette can be rewound slightly by turning the hub located on one end of its spool.

spoon.x: He must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil.

spoonful.e: From Middle English sponeful, sponefull, sponful, spone-ful, equivalent to spoon + -ful.

sporadic.e: From Medieval Latin sporadicus (whence also French sporadique, Italian sporadico, Spanish esporádico), from Ancient Greek σποραδικός (sporadikós), from σποράς (sporás…

spore.e: From New Latin spora, from Ancient Greek σπορά (sporá, “seed”), related to σπόρος (spóros, “sowing”) and σπείρω (speírō, “to sow”). Related to English spread).

sportsmanship.x: James showed good sportsmanship in consoling Shankar after his wicket fell.

sporty.x: He's perfect for me, as he's both studious and sporty.

spouse.e: From Middle English spous, spouse, from Anglo-Norman espus m, espuse f and Old French espos m, espose f and by aphesis from Latin spōnsus m (“bridegroom”), spōnsa f…
spouse.x: People should treat their spouses with respect.

spout.e: From Middle English spouten, from Middle Dutch spoiten, spouten (> Dutch spuiten (“to spout”)), from Old Dutch *spūten, *spīuten, *spīwetten, from Proto-West Germanic…
spout.x: I dropped my china teapot, and its spout broke.

sprat.e: From Middle English sprotte, from Old English sprot. Older source is unknown. Cognate with German Sprotte, Dutch sprot. Compare sprout.

sprig.e: From Middle English sprig, sprigge, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Middle Low German sprik, spricke (“a dry, easily broken twig that has fallen from a tree; sprig”).

springboard.x: The opportunity acted as a springboard for their success.

springbok.e: Borrowed from Afrikaans springbok, from Dutch springbok, from springen (“to jump, spring”) + bok (“buck, billy goat, antelope”).

springy.x: The soft peat was springy under her feet.

sprint.x: "So I broke away early this mornin', gave my guard a kick in the tummy that laid him out, and sprinted for the camp.

sprocket.e: Unknown. First attested in the 16th century. Perhaps related to Italian rocchetto (“spool”), spoletta (“spool”), sprone (“spur”), or English spoke, spike, spur.
sprocket.x: Suppose we have a widget factory that produces 100 widgets per year, and a sprocket factory that produces 200 sprockets per year.

sprout.e: From Middle English sproute, either from Middle English sprouten (“to sprout”) (see below).
sprout.x: Oh my, how your sprouts have grown!

spruce.e: From Middle English Spruce, an alteration of Pruce (“Prussia”), from Medieval Latin, from a Baltic language, probably Old Prussian; for more, see Prussia.

spunk.x: Spunk, or Touch-wood prepared, might perhaps make it Russet: and some, as Beringuccio affirmeth, have promised to make it Red.

spurious.e: Borrowed from Late Latin spurius (“illegitimate, bastardly”), possibly related to sperno or from Etruscan.
spurious.x: His argument was spurious and had no validity.

spurn.e: From Middle English spurnen, spornen, from Old English spurnan (“to strike against, kick, spurn, reject.

sputum.e: From New Latin, from Latin sputum (“that which is spit out, spittle”), from spuere (“to spit”).
sputum.x: In the early 1890s the work in the laboratory consisted of postmortems, urinalyses, and examination of sputums.

squab.e: Unknown. Possibly related to dialectal Swedish skvabb (“fatty, flabby”). First attested in the 17th century.
squab.x: Squab may be consumed by ripping the bird apart with your hands and sucking the meat from the bones.

squalid.x: Minister, I hardly think that we can exploit our Sovereign by involving her in some might call a squalid vote-grubbing exercise.

surcharge.e: From Middle French surcharge, from Old French. By surface analysis, sur- + charge. Piecewise doublet of supercharge.
surcharge.x: Our airline tickets cost twenty dollars more than we expected because we had to pay a fuel surcharge.

surety.e: From Middle English surete, attested since the early 1300s in the sense "guarantee, promise, pledge, assurance", from Anglo-Norman seurté/Old French seurté with the same…
surety.x: Know of a surety, that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land that is not theirs.

surfactant.x: It is conceivable that impairment of surfactant proteins is due to rheological and immunodefensive disorders of testis and epididymis or prostate.

surge.e: The verb is from Middle English ^((please verify)) surgen, possibly from Middle French sourgir, from Old French surgir (“to rise, ride near the shore, arrive, land”)…

surgical.x: The building was destroyed with a surgical air-strike.

surly.x: The surly weather put us all in a bad mood.

surmise.e: From Old French surmis, past participle of surmetre, surmettre (“to accuse”), from sur- (“upon”) + metre (“to put”).

surmount.e: From Middle English surmounten, from Old French surmonter (“to rise above, surmount”), from sur- (“above”) + monter (“to mount”), equivalent to sur- + mount.
surmount.x: The boiler had a large dome over the firebox, inside the cab, surmounted by Ramsbottom safety valves.

surname.e: Inherited from Middle English surname, a partial calque of Old French surnum, surnoun (“surname.
surname.x: James is my first name, and Smith is my surname.

surpass.e: From Middle French surpasser (“to pass beyond”). By surface analysis, sur- + pass. Displaced native Old English oferstīgan (literally “to climb over”).
surpass.x: The former problem student surpassed his instructor's expectations and scored top marks on his examination.

surplus.e: From Middle English surplus, from Middle French surplus. Compare French surplus.

surprisingly.x: The house was surprisingly small for such a numerous family.

surreal.x: The movie had a dreamlike, surreal atmosphere.

surreptitious.e: Borrowed from Latin surrēptīcius (“furtive, clandestine”), from surrēpō (“to creep along”).
surreptitious.x: He read the letter aloud. Sophia listened with the studied air of one for whom, even in these days, a title possessed some surreptitious allurement.

surrogate.e: From Latin surrogātus, perfect passive participle of surrogō (“to choose someone as a substitute”); a variant of subrogō, from sub (“under”) + rogō (“ask”).
surrogate.x: A mixture of horseradish and mustard often serves as a surrogate for wasabi.

surround.x: and this way they get rid of those grand and stubborn opinions that surround them.

surrounding.x: They require a surrounding which keeps them from sinking into apathy through tasks which they are able to solve and duties they can carry out.

surroundings.x: We like the way they live, in their penthouselike surroundings filled with fake ferns and goldfish.

survey.e: From Middle English surveyen, from Old French sourveoir, surveer (“to oversee”), from sour-, sur- (“over”) + veoir, veeir (“to see”), from Latin videre.
survey.x: Under his proud survey the city lies.

surveyor.e: From Middle English surveyour, from Anglo-Norman surveour, from Old French sorveor. By surface analysis, survey + -or.

survivor.x: From this moment on, I choose to live not as a victim, but as a survivor.

susceptibility.x: The eyes were large and black, and had the moonlight's melancholy, with that tearful lustre which is the certain sign of keen susceptibility.

susceptible.e: Borrowed from Late Latin susceptibilis, from Latin susceptus, from suscipiō.

suspend.e: From Old French sospendre, from Latin suspendere.

suspense.e: From Middle English suspense, suspence, from Anglo-Norman suspens (as in en suspens) and Old French suspens, from Latin suspēnsus.
suspense.x: Ten days the prophet in suspense remain'd.

sustenance.e: From Middle English sustenaunce, from Old French sustenance, from sustenir with the suffix -ance, from Vulgar Latin *sustenire, from Latin sustinere.

sutra.e: Borrowed from Sanskrit सूत्र (sū́tra, “thread, yarn, string; rule”). Doublet of sutta; more distantly related to sew and suture.

suture.e: From Middle English suture, from Latin sūtūra (“suture”), from suere (“sew, join or tack together”) + -tūra (forms action nouns).

sweaty.e: From Middle English swety, equivalent to sweat + -y.

sweeten.e: From sweet + -en. Eclipsed non-native Middle English doucen and endoucen, borrowed from Old French adoucir and endoucir (“to sweeten”).

sweetly.e: From Middle English swetly, swetely, sweteliche, from Old English swētlīċe (“sweetly; pleasantly”), equivalent to sweet + -ly.

sweetmeat.e: From Middle English swete-mete, from Old English swete mete. By surface analysis, sweet + meat (“food”).
sweetmeat.x: “Hey, sweetmeat, where you been?” Farrengalli hollered.

sweetness.e: From Middle English swetnes, swetnesse, from Old English swētnes (“sweetness”), from Proto-West Germanic *swōtinassī (“sweetness”), equivalent to sweet + -ness.
sweetness.x: At the same time, that pain is soothed by the brain’s perception of sweetness on a totally different area of your taste buds.

swerve.e: From Middle English swerven, swarven, from Old English sweorfan (“to file; rub; polish; scour; turn aside”), from Proto-Germanic *swerbaną (“to rub off; wipe.

swimmer.e: From Middle English swimmere, equivalent to swim + -er. The dumplings are so called because they are often served in stew.

swimmingly.e: From swimming (“(adj.) moving in water as an ordinary means of motion; without difficulty”) + -ly (suffix forming adverbs from adjectives).

swimsuit.x: Put on your swimsuit and let's go for a swim.

swivel.e: From Middle English swyvel, swivel, from a derivative of Old English swīfan (“to revolve”), + -el, an instrumental suffix, equivalent to swive + -el.

symbiosis.x: Bees and flowers display symbiosis. The bees get nectar and the flowers get pollinated.

symbolic.e: From French symbolique or directly from Latin symbolicus, from Ancient Greek συμβολικός (sumbolikós, “of or belonging to a symbol”), equivalent to symbol + -ic.

symmetrical.x: The building had a perfectly symmetrical façade.

sympathetic.e: Mid 17th century in the sense “relating to an affinity or paranormal influence”, from Latin sympathēticus. By surface analysis, sympathy + -etic (“pertaining to”).
sympathetic.x: John looked very upset. I gave him a sympathetic look.

sympathize.e: Borrowed from French sympathiser. By surface analysis, sympathy + -ize. Displaced native Old English efnþrōwian (literally “to suffer with or together”).
sympathize.x: President Obama in a speech this past week said that we should solve the nation's bee problem. Oh, God, we elected a guy who sympathizes with bees?

synopsis.e: From Late Latin synopsis, itself from Ancient Greek σύνοψις (súnopsis), from σύν (sún, “with or whole”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”) meaning whole view.
